screens.title: Post-Processing Effects
screens.subtitle: Enhance mood and polish by applying full-screen image effects after rendering

narration.text: Post-processing is the set of full-screen image effects applied after the scene has been rendered and right before the final image is shown. In this lesson you will learn why post-processing is used to shape mood and cohesion without overhauling every light or material. We start by installing Unity's Post Processing Stack v2, then set up the camera so it looks for volumes, and finally create Post Process Volumes and Profiles to hold effects. You will see how Bloom creates a glow around very bright areas, how Depth of Field guides attention by blurring out-of-focus regions, and how Color Grading sets a scene’s temperature and contrast. The chapter also shows how to change effects at runtime with a short script and how to avoid common mistakes that harm performance or readability. By the end, you’ll be able to add and tune Bloom, Depth of Field, Color Grading, and Vignette, place global and local volumes, and make practical optimizations to keep visuals consistent across devices. Think about one scene you want to improve visually and imagine which of these effects would produce the mood you want.

keyIdea.title: What you'll master
keyIdea.text: Install and configure the Post Processing Stack v2, create camera layers and volumes, tune Bloom, Depth of Field, Color Grading and Vignette, control effects at runtime, and optimize for performance.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll be able to verify after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives define practical skills you will build. First, you will learn what post-processing means and why it sits after rendering. Understanding this ordering helps you reason about cost and visual impact. Second, you will be able to install and configure Unity's Post Processing Stack v2, add the Post Process Layer to a camera, and assign the correct layer mask so the camera finds volumes in your scene. Third, you'll create Post Process Volumes and Profiles, choose between global and local volumes, and add effects to a profile with property overrides. Finally, you will learn to change effect properties at runtime using script references, and to optimize effects by disabling unneeded modules, lowering quality settings, and using multiple tailored volumes. Each objective links a concrete action with why it matters in practice, so you can both reproduce the steps and evaluate visual trade-offs on different platforms.

screens.title: What is Post-Processing?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and when to use it

narration.text: Post-processing refers to image effects that run after the scene has been fully rendered but before it is presented on screen. This ordering matters: because the entire frame is available, post-processing can apply global stylistic changes such as color balance, glow, edge darkening, and selective blur. Use post-processing when you want consistent, scene-wide adjustments that are expensive or impractical to reproduce by changing every light or material. For example, instead of tweaking dozens of lights for a warm, cozy tone, applying a modest color grading curve can set the temperature for the whole scene in one place. A common misconception is that post-processing replaces careful lighting and art — it does not. Over-reliance on heavy effects can hide art or make scenes look muddy. A good practice is to start with subtle values and iterate while testing across displays. When you need local variations, use volumes with colliders rather than a single global profile. Consider performance: these are full-screen operations, so apply only what contributes to the final player experience. Which global change would most improve one of your current scenes?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Post-processing applies full-frame image operations after rendering to control mood and polish with global adjustments.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › What is Post-Processing?
Definition

Full-screen image effects applied after rendering

These effects run on the final frame buffer so they can modify the entire image consistently. They are perfect for mood, focus, and polish without changing individual assets.

Why use it?
  • Set consistent scene color and contrast quickly.
  • Guide player attention with blur and vignettes.
  • Add cinematic effects like motion blur and bloom.
Common misconception

Post-processing is not a substitute for good art and lighting. Overuse can obscure detail and confuse depth cues.

Key Takeaway

Use post-processing to unify and accentuate visuals, but keep values subtle and test across displays.

Analogy
Think of post-processing like photographic filters applied after a photo is taken. You don’t move the objects; you change how the final picture looks. This is efficient for global mood shifts.
Concrete Example
To give a scene a warm evening tone, add modest color grading instead of adjusting every light’s color and intensity. The grading affects shadows, midtones, and highlights uniformly.
Check your understanding
Name one visual goal in your project that would be faster to accomplish with post-processing than by editing many lights or materials.

screens.title: Install and Configure Post Processing Stack v2
screens.subtitle: Package install, adding the Post Process Layer, and layer masks

narration.text: Installing and configuring the Post Processing Stack v2 is a short, deliberate workflow. First, open the Package Manager and install the 'Post Processing' package from the Unity registry. This provides the components and assets you will use. Next, select your main camera and add a Post Process Layer component; this component makes the camera aware of post-processing volumes. A crucial step is to create or assign a dedicated Layer in the Layers panel, for example 'PostProcessing', and then set that Layer in the Post Process Layer component so the camera knows which volumes to read. If the camera and volumes use different layers the effects will not apply, which is a common silent failure. Finally, choose a volume blending distance and antialiasing settings in the Post Process Layer as needed. Test by creating a simple global volume and adding a visible effect such as a small Bloom; this confirms the camera is correctly configured before you begin fine-tuning parameters. Install and Configure Post Processing Stack v2 means install via package manager, add post process layer to camera, assign matching layer masks, then test with a simple global volume.. In practical terms, package install, adding the post process layer, and layer masks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Install via Package Manager, add Post Process Layer to camera, assign matching layer masks, then test with a simple global volume.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Install & Configure
Process Flow

Install package → Add Post Process Layer → Assign Layer → Test

1. Install
Open Window > Package Manager, choose Unity Registry, search 'Post Processing', and install. The package supplies the needed components and profiles.
2. Add Layer
Select Main Camera, add component Post Process Layer. Create a new Layer like 'PostProcessing' and assign it to the camera and volumes.
3. Test
Create an empty GameObject, add a Post Process Volume, set Is Global and add a simple Bloom to confirm the pipeline is active.
Common pitfall
Forgetting to set the same Layer on both the camera Post Process Layer and the Post Process Volume causes no visible effect despite correct components.
Pro tip
Start with one global volume for testing, then split into local volumes as you iterate to keep control manageable.

screens.title: Post Process Layer, Volume, and Profile
screens.subtitle: How the three components work together to apply effects

narration.text: Post-processing in Unity is implemented using three cooperating parts: the Post Process Layer on the camera, Post Process Volumes in the scene, and Post Process Profiles that store effects. The Post Process Layer acts as the camera’s bridge: it listens to specified layers and applies whatever active volumes it finds. A Post Process Volume holds a reference to a Profile asset and can be global or bounded by a collider. If a volume is global it affects all cameras that include its layer; if local, it only affects cameras when they enter the volume’s bounds. The Profile is where you add and configure specific effects like Bloom or Color Grading and toggle individual property overrides. A common misconception is that profiles are attached to cameras; they are assets referenced by volumes. For a practical example, create a PostProcessGlobal GameObject, add a volume, check Is Global, create a new Profile, then add Bloom and a small vignette to see immediate results. Closing question: how would you use a local volume to create a dramatic lava cave that differs from the outside world?

keyIdea.title: Three-part system
keyIdea.text: Layer-aware camera (Post Process Layer) reads Volumes, which reference Profiles containing effect settings and overrides.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Layer → Volume → Profile
Post Process Layer
Camera component
Assign a Layer to tell the camera which volumes to read. It performs blending and applies the active profile values to the rendered frame.
Post Process Volume
Scene object
Holds a reference to a Profile. Check Is Global to apply everywhere, or leave unchecked to use collider-based influence.
Post Process Profile
Asset storage
Add effects and use property overrides so only intended values change when the profile is active.
Concrete scenario

Create a global profile with gentle color grading for overall tone. Then add a local collider volume in a cave that references another profile with stronger vignette and warm tint. As the player enters the cave, Unity blends the profiles based on volume weight, producing a smooth visual transition.

screens.title: Bloom
screens.subtitle: Parameters, visual purpose, and common mistakes

narration.text: Bloom simulates light bleeding from extremely bright areas into surrounding pixels, creating a soft glow that sells perceived brightness. The main parameters are Intensity, Threshold, and Soft Knee. Intensity controls the overall strength of the glow, Threshold sets the brightness level where bloom begins to kick in, and Soft Knee smooths the transition so highlights don’t clip harshly. Use a modest Threshold so only truly bright spots bloom; a common mistake is setting Intensity too high or lowering Threshold too far, which washes out details and flattens contrast. Bloom is excellent for light sources, emissive materials, or highlights on shiny surfaces, but it should be used sparingly. As an example, give a streetlamp a small bloom so it feels bright at night while leaving the surrounding buildings readable. When optimizing, reduce bloom resolution or quality for lower-end platforms. Closing question: which bright elements in your scene would benefit from a subtle bloom rather than a major intensity increase to your lights? Bloom means intensity, threshold, and soft knee control strength and threshold; avoid excessive intensity to prevent washed-out imagery.. In practical terms, parameters, visual purpose, and common mistakes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bloom parameters
keyIdea.text: Intensity, Threshold, and Soft Knee control strength and threshold; avoid excessive intensity to prevent washed-out imagery.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Bloom
Definition

Bloom: glow from bright areas

Use bloom to sell brightness and make highlights feel luminous. Tune Intensity for strength, Threshold for which pixels bloom, and Soft Knee to smooth the onset.

Intensity
Overall strength of the glow effect.
Threshold
Minimum brightness for a pixel to contribute to bloom.
Soft Knee
Smooths transitions near the threshold to avoid harsh clipping.
Common mistake
Excessive intensity or too low a threshold makes details disappear and flattens contrast. Start with subtle values and iterate while observing foreground detail.
Concrete example
For a nighttime street scene, set Threshold high enough that only lamps and emissive signs contribute, and Intensity between 0.5 and 1.0 to create a believable glow without losing facade detail.
Optimization
Lower bloom resolution or use a cheaper quality preset on mobile platforms. Remove bloom where it adds little to composition.
Key Takeaway

Bloom adds perceived brightness; tune threshold and intensity carefully to preserve detail and contrast.

screens.title: Depth of Field
screens.subtitle: Using focus distance, aperture, and focal length to guide attention

narration.text: Depth of Field simulates the way camera lenses focus on a plane while blurring objects in front of or behind that plane. The core parameters are Focus Distance, Aperture, and Focal Length. Focus Distance sets the plane in world units that remains sharp; Aperture controls the amount of blur for out-of-focus areas, with lower aperture numbers producing shallower depth of field; Focal Length affects perspective compression and how pronounced the blur appears. Use Depth of Field to direct the player's attention to a character, UI element, or important object while de-emphasizing background clutter. A concrete example is focusing on a collectible item in the foreground while softly blurring the background to draw the eye. A misunderstanding is to set extremely strong blur and expect players always to know depth relations; too much blur can confuse spatial cues. As a guideline, test different Focus Distances in play mode and keep blur amounts moderate so gameplay readability remains clear. Do you have a scene element that could benefit from subtle focus to clarify importance? Depth of Field means use focus distance, aperture, and focal length to blur out-of-focus regions and draw attention without obscuring gameplay information.. keyIdea.title: Depth of Field
keyIdea.text: Use Focus Distance, Aperture, and Focal Length to blur out-of-focus regions and draw attention without obscuring gameplay information.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Depth of Field
Definition

Simulate lens focus to guide attention

Control what remains sharp and what is softly blurred to emphasize elements and reduce background distraction.

Focus Distance
Distance in world units where objects remain sharp.
Aperture
Controls blur amount; lower values produce shallower depth of field.
Focal Length
Affects perspective and how blur is perceived across the scene.
Common mistake
Overusing strong blur can remove important spatial information and hurt gameplay readability. Use subtle blur to accent, not to hide elements.
Concrete example
Focus on an NPC during a conversation by setting Focus Distance to the NPC and slightly lowering Aperture. Background geometry will soften, keeping the player’s eye on the speaker.
Check your understanding
Identify a camera shot where selective focus would improve clarity and describe the focus distance you would try first.
Key Takeaway

Depth of Field guides attention; keep blur moderate to preserve spatial cues and playability.

screens.title: Color Grading and Vignette
screens.subtitle: Adjust overall mood and subtly guide the eye

narration.text: Color Grading and Vignette are complementary tools for shaping mood and focus. Color Grading adjusts the scene's temperature, tint, saturation, contrast, and lift/gamma/gain. These controls let you push a scene toward warm or cool tones, increase or reduce saturation, and alter contrast for dramatic or flat looks. Use HDR mode when you need a wider range of values. Vignette darkens the corners of the image to draw attention toward the center; change Intensity and Smoothness to tune how strong and feathered the darkening is. A concrete example: desaturate slightly and raise contrast for a gritty, tense level, and add a faint vignette so players look inward; for a cozy interior, warm the temperature, increase saturation modestly, and apply a softer vignette. A misconception is that grading should fix problems in art; color grading enhances intent, it does not compensate for poor textures or lighting. Test color grading on multiple displays because perceived color and contrast vary across monitors and mobile screens. Color Grading and Vignette means color grading sets global mood via temperature, saturation, and contrast; vignette focuses attention by darkening edges.. In practical terms, adjust overall mood and subtly guide the eye. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Color Grading + Vignette
keyIdea.text: Color grading sets global mood via temperature, saturation, and contrast; vignette focuses attention by darkening edges.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Color Grading & Vignette
Color Grading

Tone, contrast, and saturation for mood

Use Temperature and Tint for warm/cool shifts, Saturation to enrich or mute colors, Contrast to emphasize midtones, and Lift/Gamma/Gain for detailed tonal control. Choose HDR or LDR mode based on your range needs.

Temperature & Tint
Shift blue to orange or green to magenta to set warm or cool moods.
Saturation & Contrast
Increase saturation for vivid scenes, reduce it for gritty or desaturated looks.
Vignette
Edge darkening
Use Intensity and Smoothness to subtly darken corners and center the composition. Avoid heavy vignettes that cut off important UI or scene elements.
Concrete example
For a survival horror scene, desaturate colors slightly and raise contrast for grittiness. Add a medium vignette to keep the player's focus centered and heighten tension.
Key Takeaway

Color grading and vignette together shape mood and focus, but they should enhance—never hide—your art and gameplay clarity.

screens.title: Ambient Occlusion & Motion Blur
screens.subtitle: What they add and when to avoid them

narration.text: Ambient Occlusion and Motion Blur are specific post-processing modules that add realism when used correctly. Screen-space Ambient Occlusion adds subtle darkening in crevices and corners where light is naturally occluded, increasing perceived contact and depth. It is best used with moderation because heavy ambient occlusion can make scenes look overly muddy. Motion Blur softens moving objects to simulate camera shutter and speed, which can make fast action feel smoother. However, too much motion blur hurts player responsiveness and may cause discomfort; use it sparingly or limit it to cinematic sequences. A concrete example: enable screen-space ambient occlusion to enhance a cluttered interior where small crevices benefit from extra depth cues, but reduce its intensity on wide outdoor landscapes where it offers little gain. For motion blur, prefer small amounts on fast camera pans, and avoid full-screen blur in precise combat where timing matters. Always test both effects on target hardware and adjust quality or disable on low-end devices. Ambient Occlusion & Motion Blur means ao adds soft shading in crevices; motion blur smooths high-speed movement. both require careful tuning and platform testing.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › AO & Motion Blur
Ambient Occlusion (SSAO)

Adds soft contact shadows for depth

AO darkens crevices and junctions to increase perceived contact and realism. Use a low intensity for outdoor scenes and a slightly higher one for interiors or cluttered geometry.

Practical tip
Turn down AO on wide open landscapes, and prefer it on close-quarter scenes where it improves detail definition.
Motion Blur
Simulate shutter movement
Use small amounts to smooth fast motion or camera pans. Avoid heavy blur in gameplay-critical scenes where responsiveness is required.
Concrete example
Add subtle motion blur during cinematic camera sweeps to feel cinematic, but disable it during player-controlled combat to preserve clarity.
Key Takeaway

Both AO and Motion Blur are powerful when targeted; always weigh visual gain against performance and gameplay clarity.

screens.title: Scripting Post-Processing Changes
screens.subtitle: Get effect references from a profile and change them at runtime

narration.text: You can modify post-processing effects at runtime by getting references to the individual effect settings from a Post Process Profile. The typical pattern is to reference a Post Process Volume in your script, obtain its profile, and then TryGetSettings for effects like Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading. Once you have those references you can call the override method on each property to set a new value. For example, toggling bloom in response to a player action can be done by flipping the enabled override. A concrete use case is lowering saturation and raising vignette intensity when the player is low health to convey urgency. A common pitfall is assuming a setting exists in every profile; always check for null after TryGetSettings before using an effect. Also, remember that frequent full-frame changes may be costly, so smooth changes over time rather than flipping expensive properties each frame. How might you animate color grading to provide a short screen flash when the player picks up a power-up? Scripting Post-Processing Changes means reference a global volume, trygetsettings for effects, and use property overrides to change values during play.. In practical terms, get effect references from a profile and change them at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Runtime pattern
keyIdea.text: Reference a global volume, TryGetSettings for effects, and use property overrides to change values during play.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Runtime Scripting
Code Walkthrough

Pattern: get profile → TryGetSettings → Override values

Reference the Post Process Volume in a MonoBehaviour, cache the profile, and TryGetSettings for each effect you want to control. Check for nulls and avoid expensive per-frame allocations.

Best practices
  • Cache references in Start and test for null before use.
  • Smooth transitions over time instead of abrupt toggles where possible.
  • Only change what you need using property overrides.
Key Takeaway

Use TryGetSettings to safely obtain effects and override properties thoughtfully for dynamic visual feedback.

C# Example (visual only)
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Rendering.PostProcessing;

public class PostProcessController : MonoBehaviour
{
    public PostProcessVolume globalVolume; // assign in inspector
    private PostProcessProfile profile;
    private Bloom _bloom;
    private Vignette _vignette;

    void Start()
    {
        if (globalVolume != null)
        {
            profile = globalVolume.profile;
            profile.TryGetSettings(out _bloom);
            profile.TryGetSettings(out _vignette);
        }
        if (_bloom != null) _bloom.enabled.Override(false);
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // toggle bloom example shown on-screen; actual input handling belongs in your gameplay code
    }
}
Concrete example
When the player picks up a power-up, gradually increase Color Grading saturation and then fade it back. Use cached references and timed coroutines to smoothly animate values.

screens.title: Optimize Post-Processing for Performance
screens.subtitle: Practical strategies to keep effects affordable

narration.text: Because post-processing runs over the full frame, it can be expensive. Adopt a deliberate optimization strategy: first, only enable effects that meaningfully contribute to your scene. If Bloom or SSAO is barely noticeable, disable it. Second, reduce quality where available: many effects offer resolution, sample count, or quality tiers. Lower these settings on mobile or low-end hardware to regain frame rate. Third, use multiple volumes and layers to localize expensive effects — for example, apply a higher-quality profile only inside a small cinematic area and keep the global profile lighter. Fourth, avoid toggling costly settings every frame; prefer smooth, occasional transitions rather than continuous high-frequency changes. Finally, profile on target devices and iterate: visual impact and performance vary by platform, and what looks good on a desktop monitor may be too heavy for a phone. As a quick test, run the scene with and without each effect to measure its cost and subjective value. What would you disable first on your lowest-spec target? Optimize Post-Processing for Performance means disable nonessential effects, reduce quality settings, localize expensive profiles with volumes, and profile on target hardware.. In practical terms, practical strategies to keep effects affordable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Optimization checklist
keyIdea.text: Disable nonessential effects, reduce quality settings, localize expensive profiles with volumes, and profile on target hardware.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Optimization

Optimization Strategies

A set of practical rules to reduce cost while keeping most of the visual benefit.

Use only what you need
Disable effects that add little to the scene’s mood or readability.
Lower quality settings
Reduce resolution or sample counts for Bloom and SSAO on constrained devices.
Volume management
Localize expensive effects with targeted volumes instead of one heavy global profile.
Profile blending
Blend between profiles for smooth transitions, and ensure blending weights are reasonable to avoid heavy simultaneous processing.
Profile testing
Measure frame time with effects on and off on each target device to make data-driven decisions about which effects to keep or tweak.
Key Takeaway

Balance visual fidelity and performance: prefer subtle, well-placed effects and profile-based localization over a single heavy global pipeline.

screens.title: Apply Bloom, DoF, and Color Grading
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step profile creation and parameter suggestions

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks through creating a global post process profile and adding Bloom, Depth of Field, and Color Grading with suggested starting values. First, create an empty GameObject and add a Post Process Volume, check Is Global, and create a new profile asset named MainSceneProfile. Add Bloom to the profile and enable it, then start with Intensity around 0.5 to 1.0, Threshold near 1.0, and Soft Knee near 0.5. Next, add Depth of Field and set Focus Distance to place important foreground subjects in focus, Aperture around 5.6, and Focal Length around 50 as starting points. Then add Color Grading in HDR mode and try a small Temperature shift (for example minus 10 to warm slightly), a slight Saturation boost of 10 to 20, and a Contrast increase of 10 to 20. Run the scene and iterate: small changes have large perceptual effects. A common mistake is making extreme adjustments in a single parameter; instead, nudge several parameters slightly and evaluate the combined result. After testing, save the profile and consider making platform-specific clones with reduced quality for lower-end devices. What three values will you try first in your scene?

keyIdea.title: Practical setup
keyIdea.text: Create a global profile, add Bloom/DoF/Color Grading with modest starting values, then iterate and create platform-specific profiles.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Hands-on Activity
Step-by-step
  1. Create an empty GameObject and add a Post Process Volume. Check Is Global.
  2. Create a new Post Process Profile asset and assign it to the volume.
  3. Add Bloom: Intensity 0.5–1.0, Threshold ~1.0, Soft Knee ~0.5.
  4. Add Depth of Field: Focus Distance to target object, Aperture ~5.6, Focal Length ~50.
  5. Add Color Grading: Mode HDR, Temperature ±10, Saturation +10–20, Contrast +10–20.
  6. Run, iterate, and create lower-quality clones for constrained platforms.
This sequence gives you an editable profile you can refine. Small combined tweaks produce the most natural results; avoid extreme single-parameter jumps.
Concrete Example
For a cozy indoor scene, try Temperature -10, Saturation +15, Bloom Intensity 0.7, and a soft DoF focusing on the foreground actor. Iterate until lighting and materials read well together.
Quick checklist
  • Camera has Post Process Layer with correct Layer.
  • Volume references the new profile.
  • Start subtle, then increase if needed.
Key Takeaway

A small set of modest values applied consistently will improve cohesion far more than heavy-handed single settings.

narration.text: Here are three compact ideas to carry forward. First, post-processing is a post-render step that applies full-screen effects to shape mood and polish; it augments but does not replace good lighting or art. Second, Unity's Post Processing Stack v2 uses a camera-side Post Process Layer, scene Post Process Volumes, and Profile assets; matching layers and sensible profile organization are essential to predictable behavior. Third, tune effects like Bloom, Depth of Field, and Color Grading with subtle values and profile-based localization, and always test on target devices to balance visual fidelity and performance. These concepts form the backbone of practical post-processing workflows: define your visual goals, implement profiles and volumes carefully, and optimize with targeted profiles and reduced quality settings where necessary. Layer → Volume → Profile

Tune and optimize
Use subtle values, localize expensive effects with volumes, and test on target hardware.
Final takeaway

Post-processing is a high-leverage way to shape visuals. Apply it with intention, organize profiles, and always validate across devices.

narration.text: Keep three practical reminders at hand as you work. First, always match the camera layer and the volume layer so your effects actually apply; layer mismatch is the most common setup error. Second, prefer profile-based overrides: enable only the properties you need so profiles stay composable and predictable. Third, think about platform constraints early: decide which effects are non-negotiable and prepare reduced-quality clones for constrained hardware. These quick checks will save time during iteration and avoid visual surprises during testing. When you next change a profile, run a before-and-after test on your lowest-spec target to confirm the change is worth its computational cost.
